import { Aside, Check, Cite, Deeper } from "@/features/lesson/authoring";
import { TransformPlayground } from "@/courses/ast/features/transform/TransformPlayground";
import { TypeStripper } from "@/courses/ast/features/transform/TypeStripper";
import { transformExample, typeStripPresets } from "@/courses/ast/content/examples";

Every tool that changes your code starts by parsing it. Babel and codemods then take
the full route, in three steps: **parse** the code into a tree, **transform** the tree,
then **generate** code from the changed tree.<Cite id="babel-handbook" /> A tool that works
this way never edits your text directly. It edits the tree and prints new text from it.

<Aside>Smaller changes often take a shortcut: use the tree only to find *where* to change, then edit the text at those positions. ESLint's fixes work that way,<Cite id="eslint-custom-rules" /> and so did the renames in lessons 2 and 6. This lesson is about the full route.</Aside>

## Change the tree, not the text

Pick a change and look at what happens to the tree. Each one is a few lines of code that
look for a node and change a field, remove a node or replace one:

<TransformPlayground code={transformExample} />

**var → let** finds every `VariableDeclaration` whose `kind` is `"var"` and sets it to
`"let"`. That's the whole change: one string field per declaration. **remove console.log**
takes a statement out of its parent's list of statements.

<Aside>Changing the tree guarantees the new code is well-formed: every node prints as a piece of JavaScript. It doesn't guarantee the code is valid, let alone that it does the same thing. Unlike `var`, a `let` belongs to its block, can't be used before its line, and can't be declared twice in the same scope. It also can't be the whole body of an `if` without braces: `if (ready) var x = 1;` is fine, but with `let` it's a syntax error.<Cite id="mdn-let" /> None of that matters in this example, but a real var → let codemod would first check where each declaration stands, and every variable with the scope analysis from lesson 6.</Aside>

Look at **x \*\* 2 → x \* x** in particular. The code says `weight / height ** 2`, and
`**` binds tighter than `/`,<Cite id="mdn-precedence" /> so the tree is
`weight / (height ** 2)`. Swapping the operator in the tree keeps that grouping, so both
printers add the parentheses the new code needs. A find-and-replace on the text would have
written `weight / height * height`, which divides by `height` and then multiplies by it
again: the result is just `weight`. The text doesn't know which values belong to which
operator. The tree does.

The transform only does this when the left side is a plain name. Copying anything more
is risky: `next() ** 2` would become `next() * next()`, which calls the function twice.
The tree tells you what belongs together, but not whether it's safe to repeat.

## Printing it back

The tree has no blank lines, no comments in its nodes, and no memory of whether you
wrote `'single'` or `"double"` quotes. Lesson 1 called this kind of tree *abstract*. So
how can a tool print your code back without wrecking it? The two printers in the figure
take opposite approaches.

**astring** prints the whole tree from scratch.<Cite id="astring" /> The code is correct,
but your blank lines are gone, and with its default settings so are your
comments.<Cite id="astring" /> That's fine for a build tool whose output nobody reads.

**recast** keeps your original text next to the tree. When it prints, it reuses that
original text for every node you didn't touch and only prints the nodes you changed.<Cite id="recast" />
Compare the counts under the two outputs: with recast, nearly every line is exactly as
you wrote it. That's what a codemod needs, because its changes end up in your pull
request. jscodeshift, a common tool for running codemods, is built on
recast.<Cite id="jscodeshift" />

<Aside>
Formatters take the other route on purpose. Prettier reprints everything from scratch
and removes the original styling; that's its job.<Cite id="prettier" /> It still keeps
blank lines where you had them (though several in a row become one), and tries to keep each comment roughly where it was,
which its own docs call a really difficult problem.<Cite id="prettier-rationale" />
</Aside>

## Taking the types out

TypeScript is JavaScript with types added, and JavaScript engines don't understand the
types. So the most basic TypeScript transform removes them. Node.js does that for you:
run a `.ts` file and Node replaces the TypeScript syntax with spaces and runs what's left.
It doesn't check the types; it only removes them.<Cite id="node-typescript" />

Finding the types is a job for the tree. The `:` in `tax?: number` is a type annotation,
but the `:` in `a ? b : c` and in `{ name: "pen" }` isn't, and only the tree can tell them
apart. The figure parses your code with Babel's TypeScript support and blanks out every
type node:

<TypeStripper presets={typeStripPresets} />

The highlighted parts of your code are the type nodes: annotations like `: number`, the
`interface`, the `<T>` of a generic, the ` as number` and the `!` after a value. In the
first output, each of them became spaces. That's exactly what Node produces; the course's
tests compare the two character by character. It's also the shortcut from the margin note
at the top: the tree only finds *where* the types are, and the text is edited there.

Now pick **an enum**. Node refuses it, and so does the figure. An enum isn't just a type:
`Size.Small` is a real value at runtime. Removing the declaration would break the code,
and keeping it would mean generating new JavaScript, which Node deliberately doesn't do.
The same goes for namespaces with values, parameter properties and
`import =`.<Cite id="node-typescript" /> TypeScript's `erasableSyntaxOnly` option reports
those constructs in your editor, so you find out before you run.<Cite id="ts-58" />

## Finding your way back: source maps

Why spaces, and not just cut the types out? Click a word in the second output, where they
were cut. It sits at a different line and column than in your code. If that line threw an
error, the stack trace would point at a place that doesn't exist in any file you wrote.
In the first output, everything stays where you typed it, so Node doesn't need source maps
to get its stack traces right.<Cite id="node-typescript" />

Most tools can't keep everything in place. A minifier squeezes your code onto one line;
a bundler merges many files into one. So they write a **source map** next to their
output: a file that maps positions in the generated code back to the original source, so
that debuggers and stack traces can show you your own code.<Cite id="mdn-source-map" /><Cite id="ecma426" />

The map comes from the tree. Every node still carries the `start` and `end` positions of
lesson 3, so when a printer writes a node, it knows where that node came from. astring,
for example, writes a source map alongside its output, as long as the nodes carry their
positions.<Cite id="astring" />

<Check question="Which `?` and which `:` does type stripping remove here?" code={"function f(x?: number) {\n  return x ? x : 0;\n}"}>

Only the two in `x?: number`: the `?` that makes the parameter optional, and the `:` that
starts its type annotation. The `?` and `:` after `return` belong to a conditional
expression, which is plain JavaScript. A find-and-replace sees four identical characters;
the tree has an optional `Identifier` with a `TSTypeAnnotation` in one place, and a
`ConditionalExpression` in the other.

</Check>

> tools change code by changing the tree and printing it again; what they keep depends on the printer.

<Deeper about="visitors, how recast knows what changed, and what's inside a source map">

### Visitors

Real tools don't walk the tree with a loop like the figure's code does. You give them a
**visitor**: an object with a method per node type, such as `VariableDeclaration(path) { … }`.
The tool's own code that walks the tree, the **walker**, calls your method for every node
of that type.<Cite id="babel-handbook" /> Lesson 8 uses the same pattern for lint rules,
and shows what such a walker looks like.

### How recast knows what changed

When recast parses, it makes a copy of the tree for you to change, and every copied
node keeps a link to the original node through a property called `.original`. When
printing, a node that still matches its original can be printed as the original text.<Cite id="recast" />
If recast can't reuse the original text for a changed node, it falls back to a generic
printer, so the worst case is some harmless reformatting.<Cite id="recast" />

### Inside a source map

A source map is a JSON file. Its `mappings` field has an entry for every line of the
generated code, listing segments: a column in that line, plus the source file, line and
column it came from, and optionally the original name. The numbers are stored as Base64
VLQs, short text codes for whole numbers, and most are counted relative to the previous
segment to keep the file small. The generated file points to its map with a comment at
the end, such as `//# sourceMappingURL=app.js.map`.<Cite id="ecma426" />

</Deeper>
